rw: Dismissing every suggestion teaches staff that speaking up is pointless or risky, so people learn to stay quiet and stop offering ideas at all.

ww.The team offers many more ideas: This is the opposite of what happens, because people who see every idea rejected quickly conclude that contributing is futile and they offer fewer ideas, not more.
ww.The leader gains even more trust: Trust comes from consistency between words and actions; saying one wants ideas and then rejecting them all shows hypocrisy, which erodes trust instead of building it.
ww.The team grows more creative: Creativity needs a safe climate where ideas get a fair hearing; constant dismissal suppresses it, so the team becomes less creative, not more.

rw: Thanking her publicly for finishing early names the specific achievement and shows appreciation in front of peers, which is real recognition of effort and results.

ww.Giving her work to someone else without: Handing her work to someone else without telling her is the opposite of recognition, because it ignores her contribution and leaves her confused and undervalued.
ww.Ignoring her work because she is paid fo: Being paid does not remove the need for acknowledgment; ignoring her work because of salary shows no appreciation and damages motivation and loyalty over time.
ww.Taking credit for the results in front o: Taking credit for her results is a harmful behavior that steals recognition from the person who earned it, so it cannot count as recognizing her effort.

rw: Staying calm gives steady direction, priorities focus limited effort, and support helps people cope, so together they best sustain a team working under pressure.

ww.Blaming team members in public for small: Blaming members publicly for small errors adds shame and fear to an already stressful time, which lowers morale and performance rather than supporting the team.
ww.Changing the goals every hour without an: Changing goals every hour without notice creates confusion and wasted work, which increases pressure on the team instead of helping it cope with stress.
ww.Leaving the team alone to cope with the: Leaving the team alone offers no guidance or help when people need it most, so it abandons them to the stress instead of supporting them.

rw: Stretch assignments build new skills through real challenge, and regular coaching guides her growth, so together they best prepare her for a future role.

ww.Give her no feedback or any coaching at: Giving no feedback or coaching leaves her without the guidance needed to grow, so it cannot prepare a promising employee for a future role.
ww.Tell her she is not ready without giving: Saying she is not ready without advice offers no path forward; development needs concrete guidance on what to improve, which this response completely withholds.
ww.Keep her in the same job forever so that: Keeping her in the same job forever blocks growth and wastes her potential, so she gains no new skills and is not developed for any future role.

rw: Leading by example means showing through your own conduct, such as punctuality and obeying the same rules, the behavior you expect from your staff.

ww.Micromanaging staff: Micromanaging means watching and controlling every detail of staff work, which is unrelated to a leader simply following the same rules and being punctual herself.
ww.Delegating tasks: Delegating means handing tasks and authority to others; a leader following the same rules and arriving on time is behaving a certain way, not assigning work.
ww.Coercing with threats: Coercing with threats uses fear to force compliance, whereas modeling punctuality and obeying the same rules persuades through personal behavior and involves no threats at all.

rw: Asking what people think and really listening shows respect for their views and active listening, which builds trust and often leads to better decisions.

ww.A wish to delay the project for a long t: Asking for opinions and listening before deciding gathers useful input and is not meant to postpone the project; it usually improves the quality of the decision.
ww.A way to avoid making any decision at al: Asking and listening is part of reaching a decision with better information, so it cannot be a way of avoiding any decision; she still decides afterward.
ww.Weakness in the leader's judgment as she: Seeking input is a sign of strength and sound judgment, because wise leaders collect views first; it does not show she is unable to decide.

rw: Motivation moves people to act toward a goal, while inspiration lifts their sense of purpose and meaning, so this correctly separates the two ideas.

ww.Inspiration lowers effort, while motivat: This reverses the definitions, since inspiration does not lower effort and motivation is what drives action toward goals, not mainly the sense of purpose.
ww.They are exactly the same thing in every: The two are related but not identical; motivation drives action toward goals while inspiration raises purpose, so saying they are exactly the same is incorrect.
ww.Motivation comes only from pay, and insp: Motivation has many sources besides pay, such as achievement and recognition, and inspiration does not come only from fear; the two are clearly related.

rw: Recognizing their teamwork rewards the good behavior and new challenges keep them engaged, so together they keep both employees motivated and growing.

ww.Cut their pay as a punishment for workin: Cutting their pay punishes the very teamwork a leader wants to encourage, which would demotivate both employees and discourage others from cooperating in the future.
ww.Ignore their success and give them no th: Ignoring their success and withholding thanks makes people feel unappreciated, which lowers motivation instead of keeping it high for employees who work well together.
ww.Separate them so that they cannot talk d: Separating them breaks up a partnership that works well and stops useful collaboration, which would reduce motivation and results instead of sustaining them.

rw: Asking directly shows she wants honest input, and thanking those who give it encourages people to keep telling her the truth in future.

ww.Punish people who criticize her openly: Punishing people who criticize her openly teaches staff to stay silent, so she would stop receiving honest feedback instead of getting more of it.
ww.Assume everyone is happy with her work: Assuming everyone is happy gathers no real information and leaves blind spots, so it cannot give her honest feedback about her own performance.
ww.Ask only her closest friends in the team: Asking only close friends tends to produce biased, flattering answers and misses the views of others, so the feedback would not be honest or balanced.

rw: Ethical leaders treat people fairly and keep their promises, which builds trust and shows integrity, so this behavior is a clear sign of ethical leadership.

ww.Breaking rules when it is convenient to: Breaking rules when convenient shows a lack of integrity and sets a poor example, which is the opposite of ethical leadership.
ww.Favoring friends when giving out the rew: Favoring friends with rewards is unfair and shows bias, which breaks the ethical principle of treating people equally and fairly.
ww.Hiding mistakes to protect the team's im: Hiding mistakes is dishonest and prevents learning and accountability, so protecting the team's image this way is unethical rather than a sign of good leadership.

rw: Fixing the hazard protects people from harm, and telling those affected is honest and transparent, so this is the ethical choice even though it costs money.

ww.Hide it from staff and regulators: Hiding the problem from staff and regulators is dishonest and puts people at risk, so it is unethical and may also be illegal.
ww.Blame an employee for the problem: Blaming an employee for a problem that the leader found is unfair and dishonest, and it leaves the danger unaddressed, so it is not ethical.
ww.Ignore it until something goes wrong: Ignoring a known safety problem until something goes wrong risks injury and liability, and it puts cost ahead of people, so it is unethical.

rw: Leaders set direction, inspire people and drive change, while managers organize and control resources to get work done, which is the standard contrast between them.

ww.Managers never plan or organize, while l: Managers do plan and organize, and leaders do act and make decisions, so this statement gets both roles wrong and invents a false difference.
ww.Leaders only follow orders, while manage: Leaders are not limited to following orders, and managers do follow direction from above too, so this claim misdescribes both roles and is false.
ww.Leaders have no followers, while manager: Leaders do have followers, and managers do have staff to direct, so this statement contradicts the basic meaning of both roles and is false.

rw: Discussing the delay, agreeing on a corrective plan and documenting it addresses the cause, protects the buyer and keeps the relationship workable for the future.

ww.Insult the supplier's staff and threaten: Insulting staff and threatening to leave is unprofessional and damages the relationship, and it does nothing to solve the delivery problem or prevent it recurring.
ww.Cancel the contract without a word and f: Cancelling without a word is abrupt, skips any chance for the supplier to fix the problem, and may breach the contract, so it is not the best response.
ww.Say nothing and hope that it does not ha: Saying nothing lets the problem repeat because the supplier never learns it caused harm, so hoping it will not recur is not a good approach.

rw: Repeat purchases together with recommending the shop to friends are the classic signs of customer loyalty, which is a lasting commitment to the business.

ww.Customer apathy: Apathy means not caring, but a customer who keeps buying and recommends the shop clearly cares, so this behavior is the opposite of apathy.
ww.Customer churn: Churn means customers leaving or ending their business with a firm, whereas this customer keeps buying and even recommends the shop, so it is not churn.
ww.Customer complaint: A complaint expresses dissatisfaction, but this customer buys repeatedly and recommends the shop to friends, which shows satisfaction instead of a complaint.

rw: Earning $5 for each $1 spent on retention shows a profitable return, and keeping customers generally costs less than acquiring new ones, so the statement is true.

ww.Retention always loses money for the who: A $5 return on every $1 spent is a gain, not a loss, so claiming retention always loses money contradicts the figures given in the question.
ww.Retention has no effect on profit or on: Sales of $5 for each $1 spent show that retention does affect sales and profit, so saying it has no effect contradicts the data provided.
ww.New customers always cost less than exis: Winning new customers usually costs more than keeping existing ones, and the $5 return shows retention pays off, so retention is not wasted effort.

rw: Asking what she found lacking and listening carefully shows respect and reveals the real problem, which allows an appropriate fix and keeps the client's trust.

ww.Ignore the complaint and move on to othe: Ignoring the complaint leaves the client unhappy, damages the relationship and loses the chance to learn what was wrong, so it is a poor first response.
ww.Offer a refund without hearing the probl: Offering a refund before hearing the problem may not fix what she is unhappy about and could waste money, so understanding the issue must come first.
ww.Defend the report and tell her she is wr: Defending the report and telling her she is wrong makes the client feel dismissed and escalates the conflict, so it is the worst possible first response.

rw: Reputation and track record show how the partner has behaved and whether it acts consistently with shared values, so checking them first reduces risk and builds trust.

ww.The partner's advertising budget only: An advertising budget says little about whether a partner shares your values, and it should not be the only factor, so it is not the first check.
ww.The partner's office furniture and decor: Office furniture and decor reveal nothing about values, honesty or reliability, so they have no bearing on choosing a partner who shares your principles.
ww.The color of the partner's company logo: The color of a logo is a cosmetic detail unrelated to a partner's values or conduct, so it should not influence a partnership decision.

rw: A joint venture is a temporary partnership in which firms share costs, risks and profits on a specific project, which matches this three-year product arrangement exactly.

ww.A merger of firms: In a merger, two firms combine into one company permanently; here they only share costs and profits on one product for three years, so it is not a merger.
ww.A takeover bid: A takeover bid is an offer by one company to buy control of another, but these two firms are cooperating on a product, not buying each other.
ww.A franchise deal: A franchise grants rights to use a brand and business system in exchange for fees, which differs from two firms sharing costs and profits on one product.

rw: Compromise means each side gives up something to settle at a point between starting positions, which is exactly what the buyer and seller do here.

ww.Avoidance: Avoidance means sidestepping the issue without resolving it, whereas here both parties actively reach a deal, so this does not describe the situation.
ww.Competition: Competition means each side tries to win at the other's expense without conceding, but here both sides give something up, so it is not competition.
ww.Accommodation: Accommodation means one side yields entirely to the other, but here both sides give up something equally, which is compromise rather than accommodation.

rw: Interest-based negotiation looks past stated positions to the underlying needs of each side, which often reveals solutions that satisfy both parties and is what is described.

ww.Making threats to win a deal: Threats are pressure tactics aimed at forcing a win and ignore underlying needs, so they are the opposite of looking at what each side really needs.
ww.Position-based bargaining: Position-based bargaining focuses on the stated demands each side holds, whereas this negotiator looks past stated positions to underlying needs, so it does not fit.
ww.Avoiding the negotiation: Avoiding means refusing to engage with the negotiation, whereas this negotiator actively engages and probes needs, so the approach is not avoidance.

rw: Checking market prices shows whether a 10 percent rise is fair, and preparing a counter-offer gives the buyer an informed and professional position before replying.

ww.Insult the supplier and walk away from t: Insulting the supplier and walking away damages the relationship and skips any chance to negotiate, so it is not a sensible step before replying.
ww.Accept it at once without any comment or: Accepting at once with no comment gives up any chance to negotiate and may mean paying more than the market requires, so it is not wise.
ww.Stop buying forever without any discussi: Stopping all purchases forever without discussion is an extreme reaction that harms supply and the relationship, and it ignores the option of negotiating or comparing offers.

rw: One knowledgeable contact gives clients consistent answers and service because the same person understands their account, which improves customer service consistency.

ww.The price of the goods sold: A single point of contact has no direct effect on what goods cost, because price depends on costs and pricing decisions rather than who handles the account.
ww.Employee turnover only each year: Employee turnover depends on pay, conditions and management, not on whether clients have one contact, so it is not what this practice improves.
ww.The size of the main office: The size of the main office is a property decision and has no connection to how clients are served by a single contact.

rw: Follow-up is contacting a client after a sale to check satisfaction and strengthen the relationship, which matches the salesperson's action in this scenario.

ww.Prospecting: Prospecting means searching for potential new customers before any sale, but this contact is with an existing client after a sale, so it is not prospecting.
ww.Closing: Closing means securing the customer's commitment to buy, which happens before the sale is complete, whereas this contact occurs afterward to check satisfaction.
ww.Cold calling: Cold calling means contacting people who have not dealt with the firm before, but this client has already bought, so the contact is not a cold call.

rw: Paying on time shows reliability and open communication shows honesty, and together they build the mutual trust that supports a long-term supplier relationship.

ww.Hiding problems from the supplier always: Hiding problems from a supplier erodes honesty and prevents joint solutions, which damages trust over time rather than building it.
ww.Switching suppliers every week or two: Switching suppliers every week or two prevents any relationship from forming, so no trust can develop and the firm cannot rely on anyone.
ww.Delaying payments to keep cash in the ba: Delaying payments to hold cash harms the supplier's finances and shows disrespect, which weakens trust instead of building a dependable long-term partnership.

rw: Investing time in building rapport respects the client's culture and creates the trust that the client needs before discussing terms, so this is the right approach.

ww.Treat all clients the same, with no rega: Treating every client identically ignores cultural differences and can offend a client who values relationships, which risks damaging the business connection from the start.
ww.Insist on going straight to the contract: Going straight to contract terms and price disregards this client's preference for a personal relationship first and may come across as rude, harming the deal.
ww.Avoid meeting in person and use only ema: Avoiding in-person meetings and using only email works against a client who values personal contact, so it makes building the needed relationship much harder.

rw: A polite reply with an apology and an offer to fix the problem shows others the store cares and may win back the unhappy customer.

ww.Delete the review and ignore it without: Deleting the review and ignoring it looks dishonest and leaves the complaint unresolved, which can anger the customer further and harm the store's reputation.
ww.Say nothing at all and hope the review i: Saying nothing leaves the complaint unanswered in public view, which suggests the store does not care and lets the damage to its reputation grow.
ww.Argue with the reviewer in public to pro: Arguing publicly with a reviewer looks defensive and unprofessional, and it turns one complaint into a larger reputation problem for the store.

rw: Asking customers to rate service after each call gathers their opinions on quality, which is customer feedback that helps the firm improve.

ww.Hiring new staff members: Hiring new staff concerns recruitment, but rating service after each call is about gathering opinions from customers, so it is not hiring.
ww.Advertising a product line: Advertising promotes products to the public, whereas asking customers to rate service collects information from them, so it is not advertising.
ww.Price setting by the firm: Price setting decides what the firm charges, but a service rating collects opinions about quality, so it has nothing to do with pricing.

rw: A written agreement sets out what each party will do, so both know what to expect, which reduces misunderstandings and disputes.

ww.It allows either side to change terms at: A written agreement fixes the terms, so neither side can change them at will without consent; the claim is the opposite of its benefit.
ww.It removes the need for any communicatio: Communication remains necessary during the relationship even with a written agreement, so it cannot remove the need for talking and coordination between the parties.
ww.It guarantees no problems will ever aris: No contract can guarantee that problems will never arise; it only clarifies expectations and remedies, so promising no problems at all overstates its benefit.

rw: Requiring young applicants may violate age discrimination law, which protects workers age 40 and older, so this wording creates a legal concern for the employer.

ww.It makes the posting more attractive: The wording excludes older applicants, which is a legal risk and not an attraction, so it does not make the posting more appealing in a lawful sense.
ww.It is a normal requirement for all firms: Asking only for young applicants is not a normal lawful requirement, because it screens out older workers and exposes the employer to discrimination claims.
ww.It is required by law in every state: No law requires employers to seek young applicants; the law actually protects older workers from age bias, so the claim of a legal requirement is false.

rw: The Equal Pay Act requires equal pay for equal work regardless of sex, so paying a woman less than a man for the same work may violate it.

ww.The Clean Air Act: The Clean Air Act regulates air pollution and emissions, which has nothing to do with pay differences between workers doing the same job.
ww.The Sherman Act: The Sherman Act deals with monopolies and anti-competitive business practices, not with employee pay, so it does not apply to this unequal pay situation.
ww.The Lending Act: There is no federal law governing equal pay called the Lending Act; lending rules concern credit, not wages, so it does not apply here.

rw: The FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for certain family and medical reasons, which is exactly this description.

ww.A ban on all employee absences, whatever: The FMLA does not ban absences; it allows eligible employees to take leave for certain reasons, so saying it bans all absences is false.
ww.A guaranteed raise after leave, equal to: The FMLA does not guarantee a raise equal to pay lost; the leave is unpaid, so employees do not receive extra pay when they return.
ww.Paid leave that lasts for a full 12 mont: FMLA leave is unpaid and limited to 12 weeks for qualifying reasons, so a full year of paid leave for any reason is wrong on both counts.

rw: The FMLA generally requires restoring the employee to the same or an equivalent position with equivalent pay and benefits, which is what employers must do on her return.

ww.Fire her for taking the approved leave a: Firing an employee for taking approved FMLA leave is unlawful interference with her rights, so the employer generally may not do this.
ww.Reduce her pay by half on her return to: Cutting her pay in half after leave is not permitted, because the FMLA requires restoration to equivalent pay and benefits, not a punishment for being away.
ww.Move her to a worse job with lower pay a: Moving her to a worse, lower-paid job because she took leave violates the requirement to restore her to an equivalent position, so it is not allowed.

rw: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations to qualified employees with disabilities unless doing so would cause undue hardship, which is the correct requirement.

ww.Hiring only disabled workers and no othe: The ADA does not require hiring only disabled workers; it bars discrimination against qualified people with disabilities, so favoring them exclusively is not what it requires.
ww.Paying disabled workers less than the ot: The ADA prohibits discriminating in pay against workers with disabilities, so paying them less for the same job would violate the law, not satisfy it.
ww.Refusing to hire anyone with a disabilit: The ADA forbids refusing to hire a qualified person because of a disability, so it does not require refusal; it requires the opposite.

rw: The FLSA sets the federal minimum wage, overtime pay rules and child labor standards, so this option correctly states what the act covers.

ww.Tax filing deadlines and penalties for l: Tax filing deadlines and penalties are covered by tax law administered by the IRS, not by the FLSA, which concerns pay and working conditions.
ww.Product safety and recalls of faulty goo: Product safety and recalls fall under consumer protection law, while the FLSA deals with worker pay and hours, so this is not what it covers.
ww.Stock trading rules for brokers and fund: Stock trading rules for brokers come from securities law, not from the FLSA, which regulates employment standards and does not address financial markets.

rw: Regular pay is 40 x $16 = $640, and overtime is 5 x ($16 x 1.5 = $24) = $120, giving $640 + $120 = $760.

ww.$640: This figure is 40 x $16 and leaves out the overtime hours; the 5 extra hours at $24 add $120, so total pay is $760.
ww.$720: This is 45 x $16 = $720, which pays all hours at the regular rate; overtime is time-and-a-half, so the extra 5 hours add $40 more, giving $760.
ww.$800: This is too high; $800 would equal 50 hours at the regular rate, but she worked 45 and only the extra 5 earn $24, so the total is $640 + $120 = $760.

rw: Federal law protects race, religion, sex and national origin from employment discrimination under Title VII, so these are examples of protected classes.

ww.Preferred color of the staff uniform: Uniform color preference is not a legally protected characteristic, so employers may consider it freely and it does not qualify as a protected class.
ww.Favorite sport of the workers on a team: A favorite sport is a personal preference and not a protected characteristic under federal anti-discrimination law, so it is not a protected class.
ww.Favorite food of the workers in a firm: Favorite food is a personal taste with no legal protection against discrimination, so it is not a protected class under federal law.

rw: Retaliation means punishing an employee for reporting harassment or exercising legal rights, and a demotion after a report fits that definition and is unlawful.

ww.A promotion: A demotion is the opposite of a promotion, which moves an employee up, so it cannot describe punishing someone after she reported harassment.
ww.A transfer: A transfer moves someone to another role or location without necessarily harming her; demoting a person for reporting harassment is a punishment rather than a neutral transfer.
ww.A reward: A reward benefits an employee, whereas a demotion harms her, so it cannot be called a reward for reporting harassment.

rw: Sexual harassment is unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature that creates a hostile environment or ties a job benefit to compliance, which matches this definition.

ww.A friendly greeting between coworkers th: A welcome friendly greeting that makes no one uneasy is ordinary courtesy; harassment requires unwelcome conduct, so this does not define sexual harassment.
ww.A performance review in which a manager: Honest and fair performance feedback from a manager is a legitimate part of management and has no sexual nature, so it is not harassment.
ww.A discussion of a work project between t: A discussion of work tasks and deadlines among agreeing teammates is normal collaboration with nothing unwelcome or sexual about it, so it is not harassment.

rw: Documenting performance problems and following written policy gives evidence of a lawful, consistent decision, which best protects the company if the termination is challenged.

ww.Fire based on a rumor heard from another: Firing someone based on an unverified rumor is unfair, lacks evidence, and exposes the company to legal claims, so it does not protect the company.
ww.Fire without notice or reasons given to: Firing without notice or reasons offers no evidence of a fair process and invites wrongful termination claims, so it leaves the company exposed.
ww.Skip the written policy and act on feeli: Skipping written policy and acting on feelings looks arbitrary and may show bias, which weakens the company's legal position instead of protecting it.

rw: An exit interview gathers information from a departing employee on why she is leaving, which helps the firm improve retention and working conditions.

ww.Hiring a new employee for the role: Hiring a replacement is part of recruitment and selection, while an exit interview is held with someone who is leaving, so it does not hire anyone.
ww.Disciplining an employee for poor work: Discipline deals with poor performance during employment, but an exit interview is a conversation at departure to gather feedback, not a disciplinary action.
ww.Setting a salary for a brand new hire: Setting pay for a new hire happens during the hiring process, whereas an exit interview involves an employee who is leaving, so it is unrelated.

rw: Orientation, also called onboarding, introduces new hires to the workplace, policies and team, which is exactly what a tour, policy review and introductions do.

ww.A grievance procedure: A grievance procedure lets employees raise complaints, but a first-week tour, policy review and team introductions are meant to welcome a new hire.
ww.Termination of employment: Termination ends employment, whereas these activities welcome a new employee at the start of the job, so they cannot be termination.
ww.A promotion to manager: A promotion moves an existing employee to a higher role, but this is a new hire's first week, so it cannot be a promotion.

rw: Competitive pay, benefits and growth opportunities give skilled workers reasons to join and stay, so together they attract talent more than any other option.

ww.Posting no jobs and hiring no one at all: Posting no jobs and hiring no one attracts nobody, so it cannot bring in skilled workers and does the opposite of what the employer wants.
ww.Offering the lowest pay in the area to s: Offering the lowest pay in the area gives skilled workers a reason to choose competitors, so it repels talent instead of attracting it.
ww.Keeping requirements secret from all app: Keeping requirements secret leaves applicants unsure whether they qualify and discourages applications, so it does not attract skilled workers.

rw: A 401(k) match is money the employer adds to the employee's retirement account based on what she contributes, which is the correct definition.

ww.A tax paid by the worker on the money ea: A 401(k) match is not a tax on the worker's earnings; it is extra money the employer contributes, so calling it a tax is wrong.
ww.A fine for contributing too little money: A match rewards contributions and is not a fine for contributing too little, so saying it penalizes small contributions misstates how it works.
ww.A loan from the employer that the worker: A match is a contribution, not a loan, and the worker owes nothing back with interest, so describing it as a loan is incorrect.

rw: Recency effect is giving too much weight to recent performance, such as the last two months, instead of the whole year, which matches this review.

ww.Halo effect: The halo effect lets one strong trait color all ratings, but here the review leans on a recent period of time, not one trait.
ww.Central tendency: Central tendency means rating everyone near the middle of the scale, whereas this review is skewed by the timing of the most recent work.
ww.Leniency bias: Leniency bias means rating everyone too generously, but this review is distorted by focusing on only the last two months, so it is not leniency.

rw: The halo effect occurs when excellence in one area leads a rater to score every other area high too, which is exactly this manager's mistake.

ww.Central bias: Central bias means rating everyone near the middle, whereas this manager gives high marks on every item, so the error does not fit.
ww.Strictness: Strictness means rating too harshly across the board, but this manager rates the employee highly, so the error is the opposite of strictness.
ww.Recency effect: Recency effect overweights recent events, but here the high ratings come from one outstanding skill rather than the timing of performance, so it does not fit.

rw: A behavioral question about solving a customer problem is job-related, probes relevant experience and does not touch any protected characteristic, so it is lawful.

ww.'What is your religion, and which holida: Asking about religion and holidays touches a protected characteristic and is not job-related, so it is unlawful or risky and should not be asked.
ww.'How old are you, and when do you plan t: Questions about age and retirement plans relate to age, a protected characteristic, and are not job-related, so they invite discrimination claims.
ww.'Are you planning to have children?' so: Asking about plans for children relates to family status and sex discrimination and is not job-related, so it is improper even if meant to plan for leave.

rw: Training, fair pay and chances to advance give employees reasons to stay and grow, so they reduce the number of people who leave.

ww.Cutting all training and paying the lowe: Cutting training and paying the lowest legal wage gives employees reasons to leave, so it would increase turnover instead of reducing it.
ww.Raising the workload without any limit a: Raising workload without any limit causes burnout and dissatisfaction, which pushes people to quit and so increases turnover rather than lowering it.
ww.Ignoring employee feedback and exit inte: Ignoring feedback and exit interviews hides the reasons people leave, so the company cannot fix them and turnover would likely stay high or rise.

rw: A probationary period is an initial time when a new hire's performance and fit are closely reviewed before she becomes a regular employee.

ww.A permanent guarantee of employment that: A probationary period does not guarantee permanent employment, and it is typically a trial time, so a guarantee that can never be ended is wrong.
ww.A time when employees cannot be paid whi: Employees on probation are still paid for their work, so describing it as unpaid misstates what the period means.
ww.A period of unpaid leave that the firm g: Probation is a trial stage for evaluating a new hire, not unpaid leave for rest or travel, so this describes a different arrangement.

rw: Repeated policy violations after warnings are documented, job-related misconduct, and give the employer a lawful and legitimate reason to terminate.

ww.Belonging to a protected group at work: Membership in a protected group is never a lawful reason to terminate, because firing someone for it is illegal discrimination.
ww.Reporting unsafe conditions to a regulat: Reporting unsafe conditions to a regulator is protected activity, so firing someone for it would be unlawful retaliation, not a legitimate reason.
ww.Taking legally protected leave for famil: Taking legally protected family care leave is a right, so terminating someone for it would violate the law and cannot be legitimate.

rw: Workers' compensation provides benefits, such as medical care and wage replacement, for employees who are injured or made ill because of their work.

ww.Coverage for the worker's car after an a: Damage to a personal car is covered by auto insurance, while workers' compensation covers job-related injuries and illnesses, so this answer is wrong.
ww.Payment for overtime hours worked beyond: Overtime pay is governed by wage law and is paid by the employer, so workers' compensation, which covers work injuries, does not provide it.
ww.A retirement account for the worker, fun: A retirement account is a savings plan such as a 401(k); workers' compensation is insurance for work injuries and does not fund retirement.

rw: An employee handbook explains the company's policies, rules and expectations, so staff know what is required and what they can expect in return.

ww.To list customers' names and addresses: A handbook is for employees, not a list of customer names and addresses, which belong in sales or customer records.
ww.To record company profits and the divide: Profits and dividends are recorded in financial statements, not in an employee handbook, whose purpose is to inform staff about policies.
ww.To advertise products to the general pub: Advertising to the public is the job of marketing materials, whereas an employee handbook is an internal document for staff.

rw: Employers must reasonably accommodate religious practice unless it causes undue hardship, so the employer should consider the request, which is the correct approach.

ww.Fire the employee for asking to leave ea: Firing an employee for asking to leave for worship would be religious discrimination, and the law requires the employer to consider the request instead.
ww.Refuse without discussion, since hours a: Refusing without discussion ignores the duty to consider accommodation, and equal hours for all do not excuse the employer from reviewing a religious request.
ww.Ignore the request and say nothing to th: Ignoring the request fails the employer's duty to engage and may lead to a discrimination claim, so saying nothing is not appropriate.

rw: Job analysis studies a job to determine its duties, responsibilities and the requirements needed to do it, which is the correct definition.

ww.Counting the number of jobs in a country: Counting jobs in a country is labor market statistics, whereas job analysis examines the duties of one particular job within an organization.
ww.Recruiting a new worker to fill an open: Recruiting fills an open position, but job analysis comes first and studies what the job involves, so it is not recruiting.
ww.Evaluating an employee's performance for: Evaluating an employee's performance for a raise is a performance appraisal, which judges the person, while job analysis studies the job itself.

rw: Human resource planning forecasts the number and type of workers a firm needs, which is exactly what a hiring plan for next year does.

ww.Payroll processing steps: Payroll processing calculates and pays wages, so it is unrelated to forecasting how many and what kind of workers the firm needs.
ww.Performance appraisal: Performance appraisal evaluates how well current employees do their jobs, which differs from planning future staffing needs by number and type.
ww.Exit interview process: An exit interview is held when an employee leaves, so it does not plan how many workers of what type are needed next year.

rw: A wage is paid by the hour, so pay varies with hours worked, whereas a salary is a fixed amount per pay period, which is the standard distinction.

ww.A wage is a bonus and a salary is a tax: A wage is not a bonus, and a salary is not a tax; both are forms of pay for work, so this statement is simply wrong.
ww.They are exactly the same thing and mean: Wages and salaries are not identical, because wages are tied to hours worked while salaries are fixed per pay period, so saying they are the same is wrong.
ww.A wage is paid yearly and a salary is pa: This reverses the terms, since wages are paid by the hour and salaries are a fixed amount per pay period, not yearly versus hourly as stated.

rw: Dividing $52,000 by 26 pay periods gives $2,000 per paycheck, which is her gross pay before any deductions.

ww.$4,333: This is $52,000 divided by 12 months, giving $4,333, but she is paid 26 times a year, so the correct divisor is 26, giving $2,000.
ww.$1,000: This is $52,000 divided by 52 weeks, which gives $1,000 per week, but she is paid 26 times a year, so each check is $2,000.
ww.$26,000: This is half of the annual salary of $52,000, which would be right for two checks a year; with 26 checks each is $2,000.

rw: Net benefit equals benefits minus costs, so $65,000 - $50,000 = $15,000, which is the project's net gain.

ww.$65,000: This is the benefit alone, but net benefit subtracts the cost, so $65,000 minus $50,000 is $15,000, not $65,000.
ww.$50,000: This is only the cost of the project; net benefit is benefits minus costs, which is $65,000 - $50,000 = $15,000, not $50,000.
ww.$115,000: This adds the cost to the benefit, $50,000 + $65,000 = $115,000, but net benefit subtracts cost, which gives $15,000.

rw: Checking for other factors such as seasons or promotions tests whether the ad really caused the rise, avoiding the mistake of assuming cause from timing.

ww.Nothing, because the timing of the rise: Timing alone does not prove cause, because another factor could have raised sales at the same time, so the manager must test the claim.
ww.Whether competitors raised prices, since: Competitor price changes are only one possible factor, and saying no other cause could explain the rise is overconfident, so this check is too narrow.
ww.Only the cost of the ad and the fee paid: Ad cost and agency fees do not show whether the ad caused the sales rise, so checking only them ignores other explanations.

rw: Finding the original study and checking its quality tests whether the claim is supported, which is what a critical thinker does with an unsourced claim.

ww.Ignore every study ever made on the subj: Ignoring every study is an overreaction; good studies exist, and a critical thinker evaluates a specific claim instead of rejecting all research.
ww.Share it widely at once with all of your: Sharing an unsourced claim widely at once spreads possible misinformation, since a critical thinker verifies the claim before passing it on.
ww.Accept it because it sounds scientific a: Sounding scientific is not evidence; accepting a claim just because it sounds credible without a source is the uncritical behavior a critical thinker avoids.

rw: The friend's acquaintances are a small, biased sample who may share tastes, so they cannot support the claim that the phone is the best overall.

ww.The claim is proved by logic: Logic does not prove the claim, since a few people's opinions do not establish that a phone is the best, so this is not a valid proof.
ww.The claim uses many numbers: The friend gives no numbers, and using many numbers would not be a flaw anyway, so this does not describe the weakness in the argument.
ww.The sample is far too large: The flaw is that the sample is small, not large; a few friends cannot represent all phone users, so saying it is too large is wrong.

rw: Ten dentists is a tiny sample and being paid by the company creates bias, so the survey result is unreliable, which is the concern.

ww.Dentists have no opinions: Dentists do have opinions; the problem is with how this survey was done, not with dentists lacking views, so this is not the concern.
ww.The company is honest: Surveying only ten dentists paid by the company casts doubt on the claim, so the concern is bias, and calling the company honest ignores that problem.
ww.The survey was too large: The survey was too small, not too large, since only ten dentists were asked, so saying it was too large is incorrect.

rw: A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist, and the student ignores other ways to save money, so this fits the argument.

ww.Slippery slope: A slippery slope claims a small step leads to a chain of worse outcomes, but this argument offers only two choices, so it does not fit.
ww.Ad hominem: Ad hominem attacks the person making an argument rather than the argument, but the student attacks no one, so this is not the fallacy.
ww.Bandwagon: Bandwagon appeals to popularity, claiming something is right because many do it, but this argument offers only two options, so it is not bandwagon.

rw: A slippery slope claims one small step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without evidence, as when casual Fridays supposedly cause the company to collapse.

ww.Circular reasoning: Circular reasoning assumes its conclusion in its premise, but this speaker predicts a chain of escalating consequences, so it does not fit.
ww.False dilemma: A false dilemma offers just two options, whereas this speaker describes one step leading step by step to disaster, which is different.
ww.Ad hominem: Ad hominem attacks a person rather than the argument, but the speaker attacks no one, so this does not describe the fallacy.

rw: Bandwagon appeal argues something is good because many people are doing it, which is exactly the reasoning in this stock claim.

ww.False cause fallacy: False cause assumes one thing caused another from correlation, but this argument appeals to what everyone is doing, so it does not fit.
ww.Straw man fallacy: A straw man misrepresents an opponent's argument to attack it, but no opposing argument is distorted here, so it is not a straw man.
ww.Ad hominem attack: Ad hominem attacks a person instead of the argument, but nobody is attacked here, so this is not an ad hominem.

rw: A straw man distorts or exaggerates someone's position to make it easy to attack, which is what the team member does with the colleague's idea.

ww.False cause: False cause wrongly treats one event as causing another, but here the idea is exaggerated and mocked, so it is not a false cause.
ww.Bandwagon: Bandwagon appeals to popularity, while this team member distorts an idea to attack it, so the bandwagon fallacy does not apply.
ww.False dilemma: A false dilemma offers only two choices when more exist, but here the colleague's idea is distorted and attacked, so it does not fit.

rw: Concluding a plan will always work from one success is overgeneralization, because a single case is not enough evidence for a universal conclusion.

ww.Checking all of the outcomes: Checking all of the outcomes would be sound practice, but the manager looked at only one success, so this does not describe the flaw.
ww.Using sound reasoning from one case: Relying on one case is not sound reasoning, because one success does not show a plan always works, so this describes the opposite of the flaw.
ww.Using far too much data in the plan: The manager used too little data, one success, not too much, so claiming the plan used far too much data is wrong.

rw: Since all employees must wear badges and Maya is an employee, the rule applies to her, so it follows by deduction that Maya must wear a badge.

ww.Maya is the manager: Nothing in the premises says anything about who the manager is, so concluding that Maya is the manager does not follow.
ww.No one wears badges: The premise says all employees must wear badges, so concluding that no one wears badges directly contradicts it and cannot follow from the facts given.
ww.Maya may not wear a badge: This contradicts the premises, since all employees must wear badges and Maya is an employee, so she is required to wear one.

rw: Inductive reasoning generalizes from specific observations to a broader prediction, which is what the clerk does by moving from three sales to every rainy day.

ww.Random guessing: Random guessing involves no evidence, but the clerk based the prediction on observed cases, so this is not random guessing.
ww.Deductive reasoning: Deductive reasoning starts from general rules to reach certain conclusions, whereas the clerk goes from a few observations to a general rule, so it is not deductive.
ww.Circular reasoning: Circular reasoning assumes its own conclusion, but the clerk used observations to reach a prediction, so this does not describe the reasoning.

rw: Collecting data on arrivals, staffing and service times identifies where the bottleneck really lies, so it directly finds the cause of the long lines.

ww.Add decorations and signs to the store n: Decorations and signs do not affect how fast customers are served, so they cannot reveal or fix the cause of long lines.
ww.Close the store on Saturdays and open on: Closing on Saturdays avoids the problem rather than analyzing its cause, and it would lose sales, so it is not an analysis.
ww.Assume customers are impatient since peo: Assuming impatience guesses at a cause without evidence, and lines are long because of capacity issues, so it is not a real analysis.

rw: Asking why repeatedly moves past surface symptoms to the underlying root cause, so the real problem can be fixed instead of just its symptom.

ww.It shows who is to blame for the problem: The five whys aim to find the cause of a problem, not to assign blame, so this misstates the purpose of the technique.
ww.It makes the meeting longer for its own: Repeated questioning is a structured way to dig deeper, not a way to lengthen meetings, so making the meeting longer is not its purpose.
ww.It avoids needing any data from the prob: The technique still needs facts and data to answer each why, so it does not remove the need for information about the problem.

rw: A fishbone diagram, also called a cause-and-effect diagram, groups possible causes into categories such as people, process and equipment, which matches the team's list.

ww.A balance sheet: A balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and equity, so it does not group possible causes of a problem by people, process and equipment.
ww.A Gantt bar chart: A Gantt chart shows tasks over time for scheduling a project, so it does not organize possible causes of a problem.
ww.A pie chart graph: A pie chart shows parts of a whole, so it does not sort possible causes into categories to find the origin of a problem.

rw: The Pareto principle says roughly 80 percent of effects come from 20 percent of causes, which matches complaints coming from a fifth of product types.

ww.The Peter principle: The Peter principle says people rise to their level of incompetence in a hierarchy, which has nothing to do with complaints concentrated in few product types.
ww.Murphy's law of errors: Murphy's law says anything that can go wrong will go wrong, which is not the 80/20 pattern in this complaint data.
ww.The law of returns: The law of returns concerns diminishing returns on added inputs, not a pattern where a small share of causes produce most of the effects.

rw: Groupthink is when a group agrees quickly to avoid conflict, such as not wanting to disagree with the boss, which risks poor decisions.

ww.Benchmarking: Benchmarking compares a firm's performance against others, so it does not describe a group agreeing to avoid disagreeing with the boss.
ww.Brainstorming: Brainstorming generates many ideas freely, but here the group converges quickly without debate, so it is the opposite of brainstorming.
ww.Delegation: Delegation assigns tasks to others, so it is not about a group suppressing disagreement with the boss in order to agree quickly.

rw: The government's labor statistics agency collects and publishes the official data using a documented method, which makes it the most credible source for the unemployment rate.

ww.A social media meme shared by many peopl: A meme shared by many people may be inaccurate and has no verified source, so popularity does not make it credible for official statistics.
ww.A friend's guess about the job figures: A friend's guess is an unsupported opinion with no data behind it, so it is not a credible source for the unemployment rate.
ww.An anonymous blog about the labor market: An anonymous blog offers no accountable author or method, so its claims cannot be checked and it is not a credible source.

rw: Noticing the truncated axis and judging the actual size of the difference corrects the visual exaggeration, which is what a careful reader does.

ww.Ignore the numbers and the labels and lo: Ignoring the numbers and labels and looking only at the bars means relying on the misleading visual, which is the error a careful reader should avoid.
ww.Assume the chart is perfectly fair, sinc: A professional author does not guarantee fairness, since charts can mislead on purpose or by accident, so assuming the chart is fair is uncritical.
ww.Trust the visual impression that the cha: Trusting the first visual impression is exactly what the truncated axis exploits, so a careful reader should check the scale before drawing a conclusion.

rw: Option B has the highest net benefit at $6,500, which is greater than $5,200 for C and $4,000 for A, so she should choose it.

ww.Option C: Option C has a net benefit of $5,200, which is lower than B at $6,500, so choosing C would give up $1,300 of benefit.
ww.Option A: Option A has the lowest net benefit at $4,000, which is $2,500 less than B at $6,500, so it is the weakest choice.
ww.All equal: The options are not equal, since their net benefits are $4,000, $6,500 and $5,200, so B clearly stands out as the best choice.

rw: A hypothesis is a testable idea about the cause of a problem, which is checked with data and then accepted or rejected.

ww.A final conclusion about the cause of a: A final conclusion is what you reach after testing, whereas a hypothesis is a tentative idea before the evidence is gathered.
ww.A proven fact that needs no testing at a: A proven fact does not need testing, but a hypothesis is by definition still unproven and has to be tested, so this is wrong.
ww.A rule of law that governs how a firm ma: A legal rule governs how a firm may operate, which is unrelated to a testable explanation for a problem in problem solving.

rw: Believing customers will like a product without testing it accepts something as true without evidence, which is an assumption.

ww.Interviewing customers about what they t: Interviewing customers gathers real information and tests what they think, so it is evidence-gathering and not an assumption.
ww.Reading a report on the sales of the pas: Reading a full report on past sales uses actual data, so it is evidence-based and not an assumption.
ww.Measuring product sales over a year, as: Measuring sales over a year records actual results, so it produces data, not an assumption.

rw: Using the best available evidence, stating assumptions and staying ready to adjust balances speed with rigor, which is the best approach when data is limited.

ww.Flip a coin and let chance decide withou: Flipping a coin ignores all available facts, so it is a poor basis for a decision when some evidence exists.
ww.Ignore all data and follow the first ide: Following the first idea and ignoring all data disregards available evidence and risks a poor outcome, so it is not the best approach.
ww.Wait indefinitely for perfect informatio: Waiting indefinitely for perfect information means no decision is made in time, and the manager must decide quickly, so this approach fails.

rw: The urgent and important task has the greatest deadline pressure and the greatest consequences, so it should be done first according to the priority matrix.

ww.Tasks neither urgent nor vital: Tasks that are neither urgent nor important add little value and should be done last or dropped, so they should not come first.
ww.Whichever one is the easiest: Ease does not decide priority; doing the easiest task first may waste time that the urgent and important task needs, so it is not first.
ww.The urgent but not important task: An urgent but not important task is lower priority than one that is both, and it may be delegated, so it should not come first.

rw: Discussing priorities and options with the manager can lead to a realistic plan, extra help or a new deadline, so it is the best first step.

ww.Work in silence until exhausted without: Working silently until exhausted harms health and quality and gives the manager no chance to help, so it is not a good first step.
ww.Quit immediately and look for another jo: Quitting immediately is an extreme overreaction before any discussion of the problem has even been attempted, so it is not the best first step.
ww.Ignore the deadline and work at the norm: Ignoring the deadline risks failing to deliver and leaves the manager unaware of the problem, so it does not solve anything.

rw: Offering support and suggesting she talk to the manager shows concern and points toward a real fix for the overload, so it is helpful.

ww.Ignore the coworker and avoid them for t: Ignoring and avoiding the coworker leaves her to struggle alone and does nothing to help, so it is not a helpful response.
ww.Gossip about it with the rest of the tea: Gossiping spreads negativity and can hurt the coworker and the team, so it is not a helpful response to her stress.
ww.Snap back at them in front of the whole: Snapping back in front of everyone escalates the conflict and embarrasses the coworker, so it makes matters worse instead of helping.

rw: Regular sleep, exercise and breaks restore the body and mind, which builds resilience and so best manages stress over the long term.

ww.Avoiding all friends and family: Avoiding friends and family removes social support, which is important for coping with stress, so isolation tends to make long-term stress worse.
ww.Skipping meals to save time each day: Skipping meals harms health and energy, which lowers resilience to stress, so it does not manage stress over the long term.
ww.Skipping sleep to work more each night: Skipping sleep to work more reduces energy and judgment and raises stress, so it harms long-term stress management instead of helping it.

rw: Staying calm and listening without interrupting lets the customer vent, shows respect and helps you understand the billing error before trying to fix it.

ww.Shout back at the customer in the same t: Shouting back escalates the conflict and is unprofessional, so it makes the customer angrier instead of solving the billing error.
ww.Hang up the phone on the customer at onc: Hanging up abandons the customer and the problem, which increases anger and harms the firm's reputation, so it is not a good first step.
ww.Argue about the policy with the customer: Arguing about policy puts the employee against the customer before the problem is understood, which escalates the conflict instead of calming it.

rw: After listening, apologizing for the inconvenience and offering to fix the problem acknowledges the customer's feelings and moves toward a solution, which is the right next step.

ww.Say it is not your department and send t: Saying it is not your department and sending the customer elsewhere leaves the problem unsolved and frustrates the customer further.
ww.Transfer the call without any explanatio: Transferring the call without explanation leaves the customer confused and forced to repeat the story, so it does not resolve the issue.
ww.Blame the customer for the billing mista: Blaming the customer for the billing mistake is unfair, escalates the anger and damages the relationship, so it is the wrong next step.

rw: Long hours and sick days point to overwork, so she should examine workload and staffing to see whether people are overloaded.

ww.The weather outside: The weather outside has no connection to staff working late and calling in sick, so it would not explain the pattern.
ww.The staff's lunch choice: Lunch choices are unlikely to explain staff working late and calling in sick, so examining them would not address the cause.
ww.The color of the walls: The color of the walls is not a plausible cause of overtime and sick calls, so examining it would miss the real problem.

rw: Practice and preparation build confidence, and calming techniques such as slow breathing reduce nerves, so together they help most with anxiety.

ww.Avoid all presentations for the rest of: Avoiding all presentations removes the chance to build skill and confidence, so the anxiety would likely persist and could limit her career.
ww.Wait until the last minute to prepare th: Waiting until the last minute to prepare increases anxiety because she feels unprepared, so it makes the nervousness worse instead of better.
ww.Read the slides without ever looking up: Reading slides without looking up makes the delivery weak and does not reduce anxiety, so it is not an effective approach.

rw: Making a to-do list and ranking tasks by priority organizes work and ensures important tasks come first, which is a standard time-management technique.

ww.Checking email every minute of the worki: Checking email every minute breaks focus and wastes time, so it is a poor habit rather than a time-management technique.
ww.Starting many tasks without finishing th: Starting many tasks without finishing them spreads effort thin and leaves work incomplete, so it is not an effective time-management technique.
ww.Delaying all work until the deadline arr: Delaying all work until the deadline creates stress and risks poor quality, so procrastination is the opposite of time management.

rw: The Pomodoro technique uses short focused work intervals, typically 25 minutes, separated by brief breaks, which helps maintain concentration and reduce fatigue.

ww.Working for ten hours without a break to: Working ten hours without a break leads to fatigue and errors, whereas the Pomodoro technique schedules regular breaks, so this does not describe it.
ww.Working only with others in a large grou: The Pomodoro technique is about time intervals, not about group size, so working only with a large group has nothing to do with it.
ww.Working only at night, during the late h: The technique is not tied to working at night; it concerns timed work blocks and breaks at any time of day.

rw: Setting boundaries and saying no politely keeps workload manageable while preserving relationships, which fixes the problem of agreeing to every request.

ww.Quitting every job at the first sign of: Quitting every job at the first stress sign avoids the real issue and creates new problems, so it does not solve overcommitment.
ww.Hiding the problem from the manager and: Hiding the problem from the manager keeps the overload going and prevents help, so it does not solve the person's difficulty.
ww.Taking on even more tasks to stay always: Taking on even more tasks adds to the overload that already overwhelms the person, so it makes things worse.

rw: Reviewing what went wrong and adjusting the plan finds the causes and prevents a repeat, which is a constructive response to a missed deadline.

ww.Ignore the miss and carry on as before: Ignoring the miss avoids learning from it, so the same problem is likely to happen again, which is not constructive.
ww.Blame one person and move on with no cha: Blaming one person and making no changes leaves the real causes unaddressed and hurts morale, so it is not constructive.
ww.Cancel the project and drop all the work: Canceling the project and dropping the work is an overreaction that wastes the effort already done, so it is not constructive.

rw: Breaks give the mind and body a chance to recover, which restores focus and reduces errors in long work sessions.

ww.Breaks are forbidden by law at most firm: Breaks are not forbidden by law, and many jurisdictions actually require them, so this claim is false.
ww.Breaks waste time and should be skipped: Breaks do not waste time, because rest improves focus and quality and offsets the time spent, so skipping them is a mistake.
ww.Breaks cause more stress than they ease: Breaks relieve stress and fatigue instead of causing it, so saying they cause more stress than they ease is incorrect.

rw: Listening, asking questions and using criticism to improve turns feedback into growth, which is a healthy and professional way to respond.

ww.Argue immediately and defend yourself fu: Arguing immediately and defending yourself fully blocks learning and may cause conflict, so it is not a healthy response.
ww.Ignore it and pretend it was never said: Ignoring criticism and pretending it was never said wastes a chance to improve and may let problems grow, so it is unhealthy.
ww.Take it personally and sulk for several: Taking criticism personally and sulking for days harms morale and relationships and prevents improvement, so it is not healthy.

rw: Stepping in early, before conflict harms work and morale, can resolve it while it is small, so this is the right time to intervene.

ww.Never, since conflicts solve themselves: Conflicts that are growing rarely solve themselves and often get worse, so waiting for them to disappear risks damage to the team.
ww.Only after one of them has quit the job: Waiting until someone quits means the damage is already done and a valued employee is lost, so it is too late to act.
ww.Only if customers complain about it: Waiting for customer complaints means the conflict has already harmed service, so acting only then is too late to prevent the damage.

rw: A clear policy such as seniority or rotation treats everyone by the same known rule, which is fair, consistent and easy to defend.

ww.Flip a coin without a policy to avoid an: Flipping a coin with no policy seems arbitrary and does not give employees a clear fair rule, so it is a weak fair approach.
ww.Refuse both without giving any reason at: Refusing both without a reason is unexplained and unfair, and it ignores the employees' needs, so it is not a fair approach.
ww.Favor a friend or someone she likes the: Favoring a friend or someone she likes most is biased and unfair, so it is the opposite of a fair approach.

rw: Separating them calmly stops the public argument, and meeting each privately lets the manager hear both sides fairly, which is the right first step.

ww.Take sides at once without hearing eithe: Taking sides at once without hearing either person is unfair and could escalate the conflict, so it is not the first step.
ww.Join the argument and give your own view: Joining the argument and giving a loud view adds to the conflict, and a manager should model calm, so it is the wrong first step.
ww.Ignore it and walk away without saying a: Ignoring it and walking away lets the conflict continue and signals that the manager does not care, so it does not solve anything.

rw: Focusing on shared interests and exploring trade-offs finds solutions both sides can accept, which is how a stalled negotiation can move forward.

ww.Make threats to force the other side to: Making threats pushes the other side to resist or retaliate, so it hardens positions and worsens a stalled negotiation.
ww.Walk away without explaining to the othe: Walking away without explaining ends talks and gives the other side no chance to respond, so it does not break a stalemate.
ww.Insult the other side and then raise you: Insulting the other side and raising demands damages trust and hardens positions, so it makes a stalled negotiation worse.

rw: Regular meetings improve communication and coordination, and shared goals give members a common purpose, so together they would improve results for a team that works separately.

ww.More isolation between members: More isolation would reduce coordination and communication even further, so it would make results worse for a team that already rarely talks.
ww.Fewer shared goals for the team: Having fewer shared goals would weaken the team's common purpose and make members work even more separately, so it would not improve results.
ww.No meetings ever, so each works alone: No meetings means members never coordinate, which deepens the lack of communication, so it would worsen results instead of improving them.

rw: Social loafing is when a member puts in less effort in a group because he expects others to cover and no one will notice.

ww.Delegation: Delegation is assigning work to others with authority, but here a member quietly does less than others, so it does not fit.
ww.Groupthink: Groupthink is a group agreeing to avoid conflict, whereas this member simply puts in less effort, so it is not groupthink.
ww.Team synergy: Team synergy means the team achieves more together than separately, but one member slacking does the opposite, so it is not synergy.

rw: A team charter is a document that sets out a team's roles, goals, rules and decision-making process, which is exactly what this team wrote.

ww.A job resume: A resume lists an individual's job history and skills for an employer, so it does not describe a team's roles, goals and rules.
ww.A balance sheet: A balance sheet shows a firm's assets, liabilities and equity, so it does not set out a team's roles, goals and rules.
ww.A sales report: A sales report summarizes sales results, so it does not define a team's roles, goals, rules and how it will make decisions.
